why: Reader and writer pointers: a reader scans every element, a writer marks the end of the kept prefix. Because the array is sorted, a value is new exactly when it differs from the last value written, so the reader copies it to the writer slot and the writer advances.
hints: Since the array is sorted, where are all the copies of one value?
Keep w = length of the compacted prefix. For each value read, it is a new distinct value exactly when it differs from nums[w-1].
w = 0; for each x: if w == 0 or x != nums[w-1], set nums[w] = x and w += 1. Return nums[:w]. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
pitfalls: Compare with the last WRITTEN value, not with the previous read value (both work here because the array is sorted, but the writer comparison generalises to 'keep at most k copies').
Do not use a set: it costs O(n) space and the task is about compaction in place.
